Nice to get back to this for a while! In 2015 it was a surprise, from a genre I generally don't like, probably because I expected it to be one of those "Wannabe The Guy", as I called them, games whose difficulty is not based on careful design and balance but only on surprise factor. Quite the opposite: you will certainly die here, dozens of times, maybe even hundreds, but the game is always fair, everything is laid out before you, you'll get no fast ones pulled, it simply asks you to be skilled enough to pass those obstacles, and especially in the earlier levels it is also fairly generous with checkpoints.

Complementing the fine gameplay are very distinctive graphics, all in grayscale and red with fluid animations, much better than the excessively minimalistic visuals of the XBLIG original. The plot is just an excuse, but is made quite funny by the hilarious Engrish of the dialogues. And Moth being best, erm, moth.

One of those games that makes you curse, but you can't resist getting back in and try one more time.

A great 2d platformer in the vein of the classic NES Ninja Gaiden games of old. This one is actually a remake of a modest looking but really fun XBLG title (which is actually included here as a bonus unlockable!) 

The visuals are very well done and quite atractive despite sticking to use a limeted color palette mostly made up of black, white and red. The music is quite good as well with great tunes that set the current stage's given mood. Control wise is simple and responsive on gamepads as well as on keyboards, and you can even customize controls as you see fit. 

And you'll definitely appreciate the game's simple controls and its responsiveness, for this game's challenge is definitely on the tough side, so checkpoints and unlimited lives are appreciated in order to see the game's simple but entertaining story to the end.  

Speaking of the game's story, the game seems to pay an homage to the silly localization that the infamous Sega Genesis title Zero Wing got back in the day. Yup, the story is told in an intentionally silly english script that barely makes sense. Some may find it annoying, but others will definitely get a chuckle or two out of it. 

All in all, this is one of the better retro styled 2d platformer games available on steam. An easy recomendation for sure, and hey, there is now a new updated version (Mute Crimson DX) that features lots of QOL updates should you want more of what this title offers!

"Mute Crimson+" is a stylish pixelated 2D precision platformer, where you slash, double jump and wall climb your way through different levels and worlds ninja-style.
The game is pretty straightforward and simple in its execution - while there are some gameplay-mechanics which are added as you progress, your moveset never changes, every chapter ends with a boss and there is one optional collectible in every level.
Art and animation is great, the soundtrack has a banger retro vibe and the level design is really solid. Plus the story and dialogue (with nicely drawn cutscene-stills) is so purposely bad and riddled with grammar errors, it is nothing short of hilarious and amazing! (Gotta love Moth, tho!).
The game is challenging but more forgiving than other entries in the genre (unless you are playing arcade-mode with limited lives), and the difficulty curve is just right. Your jump is very high-grav and the wall grab is something to get used to, but apart from that the movement is very fluid.

Overall a great and fun entry that is worth your time!

Notes: Been a while since I played, but I don't recall having many complaints aside from the characters horizontal movement speed being a bit slow.

I'm a big fan of platformers, and Mute Crimson+ does more than enough to satisfy that itch of a tough but rewarding play-though - especially at it's $5 price tag.

Gameplay is simple: move, jump, attack - and don't die. Each World has levels that you will be testing yourself how far you can get until you can advance to that next check point. When you finally get to that next area, that rewarding feeling suddenly stops short, as you'll be dying over and over again until you reach & defeat the boss - and I found myself not wanting to stop. It's a game that's hard to put down (or close out of) and it will be difficult but also an entertaining journey for any fans with experience of these challenging platforming games. 

It's very comparable to Super Meat Boy (another brutal yet enjoyable platformer) but the controls are not as clean in my opinion. I didn't feel as if the game's controls caused the majority of my deaths, but there were a handful of times where I thought they did me in. The jumping mechanic is a bit too floaty during the in-the-air movement, the buttons sometimes did not register, and jumping onto and off edges seemed like a rough transition at times; but overall I was able to beat the game & had fun doing so. 

I thought the music was pretty good, but as with all tough platformers it can be bothersome when you're stuck at a certain stage for an hour or so. I really love the black & white colors with the red outline for the game's art style. It made objectives and hazards seem clear, and the graphics give off a retro yet new-ish feel to it. 

It is a short game but you really can't argue paying $5 for 6-8 hours of entertainment (or frustration). Time played will certainly vary with your platforming skill level - but if you are up for a quick challenge I can absolutely recommend this game to you.

+The music is awesome.
+Being able to pull off the harder levels feels fantastic.
+Game mechanics are relatively fresh throughout the levels.
+Bosses are fun.

Cons:

-The wall grapple mechanic needed work because I HATED sticking to everything I touch while mid-air; definitely made many of my deaths feel cheap. 
-Some annoying 2D side-scroller mechanics were not all that fun (Looking at you, rising lava levels).

Just so it doesn't come out of the blue, I got and played this game around the same time as The Messenger, so I mentally associate the games together and may be a little biased in saying that The Messenger feels a lot more polished than this game. I think both are faithful to the look and feel of an NES game in different ways, but I'd be lying if I said The Messenger wasn't more fun to control.

That's not to say that this game isn't excellent in its own right. This game IS polished and is a nice short action-packed adventure, and once you get used to the controls and some of the more ♥♥♥♥-ish level design, the game is pretty fun. The bosses have personality, the story doesn't take itself seriously, and everything that comes out of Mute's mouth is pure Engrish. It's funny because it's over-the-top, but that's just about the only humor in this game. The Messenger is also funny, but for its use of absurdism, deadpan reactions and awkward chemistry between characters. Actually, it's hilarious.

Both of these games are also pretty hard. If you take a look at my achievement status, you'll notice that MC+ is still incomplete, and that's because I lost motivation to pursue the last of the achievements. I would actually say both games are the same difficulty, and that's because I draw a line between difficulty and tedium. You could say that MC+ is harder because I can't find the motivation to do an arcade mode run, whereas I 100%'d The Messenger, but the fact is, I still did beat both games. The problem is that arcade mode boots you back to the main menu after 9 deaths, in a game where it's easy to die dozens of times in one area. That's not difficulty. That's tedium. It's tedious because if you game over on the third world, that means you have to re-do worlds 1-2 just to get back to where you were. Hence I don't feel like doing that, hence I lose motivation. I don't like MC+'s arcade mode.

I apologize for comparing this to a much larger and unrelated game sharing only the themes of 'retro homage' and 'ninja protagonist'. Again, I'm a little biased. But I feel confident in saying that both games are worth their respective prices, and that I recommend both of them.

Retro-style platformers are a dime a dozen, and lots of them have great mechanics but still end up being boring just because the levels are boring. The hit detection on some obstacles felt a little wonky in places, but it's a very minor complaint. Overall it's a great playthrough. Highly recommended.

It's not a horrible game, especially for the price, but I wouldn't recommend it to my friends. The graphics are very pleasing and the retro aesthetic is well executed. But my big gripe about it is that the controls are very stiff, and almost all of it's difficulty and frustration stems from the stiff controls, rather than challenging enemies or level design.

Most of the levels and jumps I think would be easy if the control was fluid like Mario or Shantae and the Pirate's Curse, for examples. But your character has no weight or momentum and things such as climbing up a wall and getting to stand at the top of that wall make you have to circle jerk the analog stick just right to hit a precise angle to climb over the corner of the top block. Up climbs up and left or right makes him get on top of the ledge, but you need to have him at the right spot for him to get on. And so many jumps require you to cilmb up or down walls and fall off them to jump to the next platform. The biggest example of this is the levels where lava rises. Obstacles include singular floating coulmns of walls you climb up/down, fall off then hit jump in mid air at the right spot to land on the next platform, all before the lava gets you. But he never wants to fall off or climb onto the top while he's climbing the walls. It's as if he's glued to the walls, and it feels awkward the way you have to move the joystick to do it right. It feels like an interruption rather than another movement.

Jumps feel weird, it always feels like you're gonna miss a platform but you make it anyways, and other times you need precise timing when to double jump, but the lack of momentum makes you under estimate the jump, because it feels like it should put you higher but it doesn't. It's hard to explain but it's noticable to feel when playing. The jump mechanics are not satisfying. All of the level design and enemies are based around the awkward controls it seems. The game is very much a nod to Ninja Gaiden, But even Ninja Gaiden's controls were fluid, responsive, and satisfying. It's like the game opted out Ninja Gaiden's BS enemy placement  and replaced it with awkward controls.

Another thing that feels weird is attacking while in the air. You need to hit the attack button slightly before you get close to the enemy, because of his swing animation, but if you do it when you're too close, the hit won't register fast enough. And too close doesn't mean when you're already on top of the enemy, it still looks like there's plenty of room for your attack. So then instinct makes you want to hit the attack button too early, since  the animation shows him bringing the sword down the entire time in the air after the button's pressed until he lands, so you think the sword touching the enemy will count, but it doesn't and that kills you too. It's such a counterintuitive timing, and fairly easy once you get used to the weirdness of it, but again it makes for a non-fluid, non-flowing gameplay.

Another annoyance is the dialogue. Whoever wrote it thought the "All your base are belong to us" meme was way too funny and misuses grammar intentionally in every sentence. It becomes borderline racist, making you wonder if they're doing it because they're trying to play off a stereotypical ninja, but I just think they find gibberish that funny. Instead it makes me dread the cutscenes.

All in all, it's not a bad game. If you want an inexpensive game with a retro, nostalgic feeling and are running out of others on steam, this may be for you. But do keep in mind the controls and gameplay before buying. It takes some getting used to.

I can't tell if the dialogue is intentionally bad to evoke the poorly translated games on the NES, or if it's actually just a terrible translation. Either way, it makes an already super plain story even more unbearable.

On top of that, the game is pretty middling. The controls are sometimes not as precise as you want them to be, and sometimes you'll end up doing something you didn't intend to, such as stick to a block when you wanted to get on top of it, or jump slightly higher than you intended to. There's also a general lack of momentum to your character's movement, so every jump feels very stiff and rigid.

The level design is alright, with each world featuring some new game mechanic. The second world features wind, another world introduces teleporters. However, each world feels liek it goes on for a bit too long, and can sometimes get a little repetitive.

The art ranges from acceptable to pretty bad. Even considering this is a throwback title, there are areas where it looks like the art was made in MS Paint using the spray tool. The design of the main character is fairly bland as well, but I will say that he animates nicely. The bosses also all look pretty good and animate well.

Music is good, too.

At some points, I had a good time with the game, but at other points it felt very draining and frustrating. However, this frustration was not the good kind, it came from the less than ideal controls and the repetitive nature of some worlds. It's not the worst game, but I would say that unless you're really desperate for a retro platformer and you've already exhausted the many other options out there, that you should steer clear of this one.

I loved the original Xbox Indie Mute Crimson, but I held off on picking this remake up since, well, I figured I already bought and played it. Took my little blocky caterpillar ninja through his high contrast world, gathered all of the coins, and liked it enough to publish a poorly written review for my Xbox Indie site. I didn't see much reason to return.

I was wrong. The big improvement here are certainly the graphics. The old shoebox now looks like an actual ninja guy. The scant enemies and levels look much better and animate smoothly. We now can enjoy some impressive cinematic art between levels as well, and everything just pops. For a game with a mostly two color palette, it looks really good. Kinda like a 2-D MadWorld. Well, maybe not, but it oozes style.

Platforming is tight and a joy to play. If you're like me, then you're a fast approaching middle-aged white guy, but then you'd also find the level design strict and at times maddening but always fair. You'd also hate the rising lava levels which Mute Crimson+ employs on occasion, stressing out our fat middle-aged hearts to dangerous limits. Welcomed modern conveniences of infinite lives and checkpoints will help keep your sanity intact, though they're far from a crutch. An optional goal of finding hidden coins in a level provide further challenge, and it can be tough to secure it and make it out alive.

There's still a bit of clunkiness present what with the inexplicable arrow zones which alter the control of the ninja, but these spots add some much needed variety to the game and help flesh out a journey otherwise dominated by jumping and slashing. I'm so glad there are people out there who remember that platformers can exist between the extremes of masochist memorization and cakewalk adventure fetch-quests. Mute Crimson+ feels so refreshing by comparison, even after playing the XBLIG original. It's not going to blow anyone away, but it's an immensely satisfying game all the same.

Almost everything in this game works together to create a compelling platforming experience.

Enemies are placed rarely as challenges in themselves but usualy as accents for the platforming that force you to think more about timing or positioning.  The color scheme really makes the levels, platforms, and hazards pop and is always well excecuted.  New platforming elements are introduced often and iterated on many times to create a challenging but fair difficulty curve.  The best bosses in the game put your platforming skills to a huge test and are extremely satisfying to take down.  The dialogue is hilarious but short enough to keep a good pace in the game.

Overall a really great platformer, retro-style game, and game in general.

I had a lot of fun playing Mute Crimson+. In my opinion, it's a pretty successful tribute to the NES era. 

I loved the artistic direction. The music was really great, and the overall graphic style was really polished. I've rarely seen such wonderful boss sprites in that kind of games too. Also, the cutscenes are hilarious.

Gameplay-wise, the game is neat too. It has a very inspired level design, and is just as compelling and difficult as we expect from a retro-ish platformer. Always tight, never cheap. The final boss battle was both badass and intense too, which I think is one of the most solid arguments for a game of this kind.

Finally, the game has lots of nice features, such as a boss rush, an arcade mode and a time attack, which adds a little to a lot of replayability to it, depending on what kind of player you are.

Basically, Mute Crimson+ is a really solid old-school platformer, and I definitely recommend it.

The graphical style is neat and original, reminiscent of some DOS games (I know it's going for NES style, but it kind of falls short in that avenue). The concept is not bad, it's obviously a parody/homage of Ninja Gaiden and there's nothing wrong with that. And it's tough being a developer, and you can't please everyone. I didn't like this game, but I always feel bad leaving bad reviews on indie games. Anyway, here are some facts and opinions:

▬ PROS ▬
- Decent DOS-y / NES-y graphics
- Cool blood physics effects and stuff
- Get double jump from the beginning (I love jumpin)
- Wall climbing is always fun
- Lots of checkpoints
- No lives (they know the game is hard)
- Collectibles are mostly well placed

▬ CONS ▬
- Rigid jumping physics make for annoying platforming
- Unoriginal and Difficult to read enemy design
- Wind
- Walls are too clingy (often accidentally grab onto walls and get killed)
- High contrast graphics hard on eyes after a while
- Bosses are uninspired and not very fun
- Wind
- Spikes on pretty much every surface
- No powerups (at least as far in as I played. If the game doesn't have anything but jumping within the first 20 minutes it's too dry for me)
- No real original mechanics or well-adapted borrowed mechanics
- Wall jumping is wonky and often leads to death
- Poor enemy AI
- etc etc etc

I'm not sure what advice I'd give to the developers to improve the game without changing the vision of the game. I'm not sure if this is how the game is intended to be. These are some things I'd be interested in:

- More enemies, but you have a weak projectile (shuriken)
- Maybe some enemies have projectiles but you can deflect them?
- Some kind of ground/air dash for mobility and attacking
- Less stiff jumping (gradually slow as you reach jump apex, then slowly but exponentially increase fall speed. You know, how gravity works)
- Make dying constantly not a huge element of the game (personal preference - repetition is not always fun)
- Maybe an ability system like the lantern items from Ninja Gaiden
- Maybe couch co-op mode with even more enemies?
- Get rid of the wind (sorry, I've hated wind mechanics in platformers since Lost Levels)

If you're reading this, Dev, keep making games! Don't ever get discouraged!
